title: Janmashtami: the universe in a baby's mouth
hookLine: a whole house awake at midnight for a baby, and the day his mother saw the universe in his mouth
carry: vatsalya: loving the infinite god as a child
last: NAVARATRI: HONORED AT YOUR OWN TABLE.

cards: It's eleven forty-five at night, and nobody in the house is asleep. Grandma hasn't eaten since morning. In the corner is a tiny wooden cradle hung with flowers, and in it a little image of a baby.
The temple down the road is packed, singing the same few lines louder as the minutes pass. At midnight, the conch shells blow and everyone shouts. This is Janmashtami, Krishna's birth.
You've heard the night he was born. Today, a story about the baby, and why a house rocks a cradle for God.

teach.b: Krishna, born at midnight in a king's prison, was carried across the river and raised in Gokul by Yashoda, the cowherd woman who loved him as her own. One day the other children run to her: Krishna's been eating dirt!
Yashoda grabs him. Open your mouth. He says he didn't do it; they're telling tales.
Open it, she says. He opens it.

And inside that little mouth she sees everything: the sky and the stars, the earth with its mountains and oceans, fire and wind, time itself, and her own village, and herself, standing there, looking into his mouth.
She's terrified. Is this a dream? Then, the story says, Krishna lets the vision fade, and she forgets it.
She just sets him on her lap, her boy again. That's from the Bhagavata Purana, and it holds the teaching under Janmashtami.

teach.h: VATSALYA: A PARENT'S LOVE, GIVEN TO GOD.
teach.b: Hindus call this kind of love vatsalya, a parent's tender love, offered to God. The God who holds the universe lets himself be loved like a baby: fed, bathed, scolded, rocked to sleep.
Many teachers say Yashoda's love is sweeter to God than all the awe in the world. So on Janmashtami, families don't only bow. Many fast and stay awake singing until midnight, the hour he was born.
Then baby Krishna is bathed like a newborn in panchamrita, the five nectars: milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar.

teach.h: THE BATH, THE CRADLE, THE PUSH.
teach.b: He's dressed in new clothes and laid in the cradle, and people take turns giving it a push.

teach.h: THE INFINITE, SMALL ENOUGH TO HOLD.
teach.b: The infinite God, small enough to hold.

how: On Janmashtami many Hindus fast until midnight, sing and retell Krishna's birth in homes and temples, and at midnight bathe an image of baby Krishna in panchamrita, dress him, and rock him in a cradle before breaking the fast; many homes care for a baby Krishna image all year.

Krishna's wedding day, kept with a great feast

games.q: what's inside the midnight — tap the pairs.
p: the five nectars for the baby's bath
a parent's tender love, offered to God

s: the Janmashtami fast is a punishment
it's waiting with your body, from morning until the midnight birth.
Yashoda saw the whole universe inside baby Krishna's mouth
then the vision faded, and she just held her boy again. that's vatsalya: the infinite God, loved as a child.
baby Krishna is bathed at midnight
in panchamrita: milk, yogurt, honey, ghee and sugar. then new clothes, and the cradle.

games.q: you're Yashoda. the kids say Krishna ate dirt, so you look in his mouth and see the whole universe. what happens next?
o: you bow down and never dare touch him again.
the vision fades, and you scoop him onto your lap.
you send him off to live at the temple.
games.why: the vision fades and Yashoda simply loves him as her boy. Janmashtami's cradle keeps that love: the infinite God, rocked like a baby.

practice: Picture that tiny cradle hung with flowers and give it one small push: breathe out as it swings away, in as it comes back, gently, because there's a newborn in there, and the universe with him.
If you pray, say Krishna's name with each swing. If not, keep the rhythm, and think of someone small you care for.

wordCard.voice: Janmashtami. Krishna's birth, on the eighth day of the dark half of the month, kept with a fast, a vigil, and a cradle rocked at midnight.

orig.note: Sanskrit: janma, birth, and ashtami, the eighth day of the lunar fortnight.

carryVoice: Your line: vatsalya. Loving the infinite God as a child. Midnight comes when it comes. See you tomorrow.
